subject: body odour and sweat
title: What If You Never Wore Deodorant?

scenes.text: What if you never wore deodorant? Your sweat wouldn't be the problem. It barely smells at all.
At puberty, glands in your armpits switch on and start releasing a thicker, oily kind of sweat.
Bacteria living there, like Staphylococcus hominis, break that sweat down into sulfur compounds that smell like onions.
Your nose detects them at a few parts per billion, like two drops of ink in a backyard pool.
But in one British study, about 2 percent of people carried a gene variant that starves those bacteria.
In much of East Asia, that variant is the norm. Yet over three quarters of the odour-free Britons still used deodorant almost daily.

description:
What if you never wore deodorant? Fresh sweat is almost odourless: underarm bacteria such as Staphylococcus hominis turn it into pungent sulfur compounds.
About 2% of the 6,495 women in a University of Bristol study carried an ABCC11 gene variant that means almost no underarm odour, the norm in much of East Asia, yet 78% of them still used deodorant on all or most days.
